newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Japan said likely to compromise in Jakarta car row.
newsitem.headline: Japan said likely to compromise in Jakarta car row.

text.p: Japan is likely to compromise on Indonesia's controversial national car after a first batch of more than 2,000 of the Korean-built vehicles arrived in Jakarta this week, a leading Indonesian economist said on Friday.

"I don't think the Japanese will sacrifice the bigger relationship in order to have a solution in this car conflict," economist Christianto Wibisono, director of Indonesian Business Data Centre, said.
"They will try to negotiate," he told Reuters.

Japan has threatened to take Indonesia to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) over its national car policy which allows only PT Timor Putra Nasional to import vehicles free of tariffs and luxury taxes imposed on other car makers.
Timor Putra, controlled by President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra, has established a joint venture with South Korea's Kia Motors Corp to produce the cars.
The policy has also been condemned by the United States and the European Union as breaking WTO rules.
The cars are being imported from South Korea until production facilities are ready in Indonesia.
A diplomat at the Japanese embassy in Jakarta, who asked not to be named, confirmed the embassy had reported the arrival of the cars.
"We are still doing some fact-finding regarding the arrival of the Timor cars and its treatment by the Indonesian government," the diplomat said.
PT Timor spokesman Mohamad Ircham said the cars in the first batch met government requirements.
"They are all of the one type, S515 with 1,500 cc single overhead cam, the standard vehicle which we will market," Ircham said.
"About 8,000 have been ordered by the public. They have paid a deposit of 3.5 million rupiah of an off-the-road basic price of 33 million rupiah," he told Reuters.
PT Timor hopes to sell up to 40,000 cars after they hit the market in October.
PT Timor will start with 10 dealers in the greater Jakarta area and 20 authorised repair shops, Ircham said.
